cards.title: How neurons learn different patterns
cards.body: Each beaker receives input through different taps. A tip holds its rivals back. Over time, the taps change, so different beakers respond to different patterns.

diagram.title: Inside the learning network
diagram.caption: One winner’s feedback is shown. Simplified from Diehl & Cook (2015). Tap a mechanism to see its role.

items.label: Input spikes
items.note: Pixel intensity sets input spike rates.

items.label: Competition
items.note: Excitatory neurons recruit inhibition that suppresses rivals.

items.label: STDP
items.note: Spike timing changes the incoming weights; no digit labels guide these updates.

items.label: Thresholds
items.note: Frequent firing raises the threshold, reducing repeated wins.

cards.title: How the network learns a pattern
cards.body: A neuron responds strongly to a pattern. STDP changes its incoming connections, making that pattern easier to recognize next time. Inhibition limits rival responses; a rising threshold makes it harder for the same neuron to keep winning.

cards.title: Learning weights comes before naming neurons
cards.body: First, STDP changes the connections without digit labels. Then labeled examples are used to name each neuron by the digit it responds to most. Naming a neuron does not train its connections.

quiz.prompt: Which mechanism shapes the winner’s incoming template?
quiz.why: Timing-dependent synaptic updates learn the receptive field.

quiz.prompt: Which statements describe the learning setup?
quiz.why: Unsupervised weight learning is followed by label assignment for evaluation.

cards.title: A value shared across neurons
cards.body: A single beaker need not carry the entire value. Several neurons prefer different values, with overlapping responses. Their collective pattern carries the estimate.

diagram.title: More response means more influence
diagram.caption: Preferences are 2 and 8; response weights are 3 and 1. The weighted estimate is 3.5.

cards.title: Let several neurons vote
cards.body: Two neurons prefer 2 and 8. Their response weights are 3 and 1. Weighted-average decoding gives (3×2 + 1×8)/(3+1) = 3.5.

cards.title: Checkpoint · make the connections
cards.body: Keep the state variables separate: the delta reference remembers sent events; adaptation remembers previous spikes; recovery shapes future voltage dynamics.

diagram.title: Keep the memories separate
diagram.caption: Ask what a state remembers before updating it.

cards.title: Which state changes at a spike?
cards.body: Before calculating, name what gets updated and what stays fixed. A reset of voltage is different from a jump of recovery or threshold.

quiz.prompt: r = 50, θ = 1, reading = 48.7. New reference after one event?

quiz.prompt: Baseline θ₀ = 1, a = 0.5, ρ = 0.8. Threshold after two silent steps?
quiz.why: Keep 80% of the extra twice, then add baseline.

quiz.prompt: At an Izhikevich spike, which updates occur?
quiz.why: Voltage resets; recovery receives an additive jump.
